sheets.name: Scenario I - Uncertainties

cells.value: Increased jellyfish biomass scenario re-run under different assumptions of parameter uncertainty. Jellyfish biomass was increased by 50% and results are reported as the mean and coefficient of variation (CV) of the relative change in production (fractional change = (Pscenario model - Pbase model) / Pbase model) of 1000 randomly generated models.

Models were randomly generated by drawing from a normal distribution about each element of the ECOTRAN production matrix. The level of uncertainty about each production matrix element is calculated from the uncertainty of each parameter (biomass, P/B, P/Q, AE, diet, landings, and discards) defined in the model pedigree (Table J).

In this alternate uncertainty analysis, scenarios were re-run with the uncertainty of biomass, growth efficiency (P/Q), and diet terms each separately decreased by a factor of 0.1 and then run with uncertainties increased by a factor of 10.

To summarize differences under alternate levels of uncertainty, we looked at the change in the mean scenario effect and the spread of scenario effects as the ratio of the high uncertainty run to the low uncertainty run (ratios of mean effect and spread of effects under 10X increased uncertainty / 0.1X decreased uncertainty)
Changes of 0.5 or greater are highlighted. Decreased mean effects under higher uncertainty are in red. Increased mean effects under higher uncertainty are in green.
Increased uncertainty generally reduced the scale of the mean scenario effect but increased the spread of the scenario effect.

The main reason for the reduced mean effect under greater uncertainty is that a greater fraction of the 1000 Monte Carlo models could not support the full targeted 1.5X increase in jellyfish or in forage fish biomasses.
The system was generally more sensitive to uncertainty in growth efficiency (P/Q) than to uncertainty in biomass or uncertainty in diet.
Change in MEAN effect (10X increased uncertainty / 0.1X decreased uncertainty)
Change in SPREAD effect (10X increased uncertainty / 0.1X decreased uncertainty)
